edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 2, Paris 1844), De corona militis, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Puta denique licere militiam usque ad caussam coronae. Sed et de corona prius dicamus. Laurea ista Apollini vel Libero sacra est: illi, ut deo telorum; huic, ut deo triumphorum. Sic docet Claudius cum et myrto ait milites redimiri solere. Veneris enim myrtum, matris Aeneae, non laurum, etiam amiculae Martis, per Iliam et Romulos Romani. Sed ego Venerem non credo ex hac parte cum Marte Romanam, qua pellicis dolor est. Quum et olea militia coronatur, ad Minervam est idololatria, armorum aeque deam, sed et paci cum Neptuno initae ex hac arbore coronatam. In his erit serti militaris superstitio polluta et polluens, omniaque jam polluentur et caussis. Ecce annua votorum nuncupatio quid videtur? prima in principiis, secunda in capitoliis. Accipe post loca et verba: Tunc Tibi, Jupiter, Bove Cornibus Auro Decoratis Vovimus Esse Futurum. Cujus sententiae vox est? utique negationis. Etiamsi tacet illic Christianus ore, coronatus capite respondit. Eadem laurea in donativi dispensatione denuntiatur plane non gratuita idololatria, aliquibus aureis venditans Christum, ut argenteis Judas. Hoc erit, Non potestis Deo servire et mammonae: mammonae manum tradere, et a Deo absistere? Hoc erit, Reddite quae sunt Caesaris Caesari, et quae Dei Deo: nec hominem Deo reddere, et denarium Caesari auferre? Triumphi laurea foliis struitur, an cadaveribus? lamnis ornatur, an bustis? unguentis delibuitur an lacrymis conjugum et matrum? Fortasse quorumdam et Christianorum: et apud barbaros enim Christus. Qui hanc portaverit in capite caussam, nonne et ipse oppugnavit? Est et alia militia regiarum familiarum. Nam et castrenses appellantur munificiae, et ipsae solemnium Caesareanorum. Sed et tu proinde miles ac servus alterius es: et si duorum, Dei et Caesaris, certe tunc non Caesaris, cum te Deo debes, etiam in communibus, credo, potiori.
pass_a_gloss: Suppose finally it is permitted military service up to the cause of the crown. But also let us speak about the crown beforehand. That laurel is sacred to Apollo or to Bacchus: to him, as the god of missiles; to this one, as the god of triumphs. Thus Claudius teaches when he also says that soldiers are accustomed to be redeemed with myrtle. For myrtle is of Venus, the mother of Aeneas, not laurel, and also of the lovers of Mars, through Iliam and Romulus the Romans. But I do not believe Venus is on the side of the Romans with Mars, where there is the pain of skin. When also the olive tree crowns military service, it is idolatry to Minerva, equally the goddess of arms, but also of peace, begun with Neptune, crowned from this tree. In these things the superstition of the military garland will be polluted and polluting, and all things now will be polluted and causes. Behold the annual announcement of vows, what does it seem? first in beginnings, second in chapters. Receive after places and words: Then to You, Jupiter, with a Bull with Golden Horns we vow to be future. What is the voice of this sentence? certainly of negation. Even if the Christian is silent there with his mouth, the crowned head responds. The same laurel in the dispensation of donatives is plainly announced, not gratuitous idolatry, selling Christ to some with gold, as Judas with silver. This will be, You cannot serve God and mammon: to hand over the hand to mammon, and to abstain from God? This will be, Render what are Caesar's to Caesar, and what are God's to God: nor to render man to God, and to take away the denarius from Caesar? The laurel of triumphs is constructed with leaves, or with busts? It is adorned with lamina, or with statues? It is anointed with ointments or with the tears of wives and mothers? Perhaps of some Christians also: and Christ is also among the barbarians. Who will have borne this cause on his head, will he not also have fought against it? There is also another military service of royal families. For also the castrenses are called munificences, and they themselves are of the solemnities of the Caesareans. But you are also accordingly a soldier and a servant of another: and if of two, of God and Caesar, certainly then not of Caesar, when you owe yourself to God, even in common things, I believe, to the more important one.

rejected: Adorned with lambs or with tombs
choices.why: lamnis is the dative or ablative plural of lamina, which means a thin plate or sheet of metal
unguentis is the dative or ablative plural of unguentum, which means ointment or perfume

choices.english: with the tears of wives and mothers
choices.why: lacrymis is the dative or ablative plural of lacrima, which means tear
Deo is the dative of Deus, which means God

bible_refs.note: You cannot serve God and mammon
Render what are Caesar's to Caesar, and what are God's to God

pass_b_english: Suppose, finally, that military service is permitted up to the point of the crown. But let us speak first about the crown itself. That laurel is sacred to Apollo or to Bacchus: to the one, as god of missiles; to the other, as god of triumphs. So Claudius teaches when he says that soldiers are also accustomed to be crowned with myrtle. For myrtle belongs to Venus, mother of Aeneas, not laurel — and also to the lovers of Mars, through Ilium and the Romuli of the Romans. But I do not believe Venus stands on the Romans' side with Mars, where the pain of flaying lies. When the olive also crowns military service, it is idolatry to Minerva, equally goddess of arms, but also of peace, established with Neptune from this tree. In these things the superstition of the military garland is polluted and polluting, and now all things will be polluted — causes included. Look at the annual declaration of vows: what does it look like? First at the principia, second at the capitolia. Take the places and the words: 'Then to you, Jupiter, with a bull with gold-adorned horns, we vow to be future.' Whose voice is that sentence? Certainly the voice of negation. Even if the Christian is silent there with his mouth, the crowned head answers. The same laurel, in the distribution of donatives, is plainly declared not to be gratuitous idolatry, selling Christ to some for gold, just as Judas did for silver. This will be: 'You cannot serve God and mammon' (Luke 16:13) — to hand yourself over to mammon and withdraw from God? This will be: 'Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's' (Matthew 22:21) — not to render a man to God, and to snatch the denarius away from Caesar? Is the laurel of triumphs constructed with leaves, or with corpses? Is it adorned with lamina, or with busts? Is it anointed with ointments, or with the tears of wives and mothers? Perhaps even of some Christians: for Christ is also among the barbarians. Whoever has borne this cause on his head, has he not also fought against it? There is also another military service, that of royal households. For the castrenses are called munificences, and they themselves belong to the solemnities of the Caesareans. But you, accordingly, are a soldier and a servant of another: and if of two, God and Caesar, then certainly not of Caesar, when you owe yourself to God, even in common matters, I believe, to the more important one.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful gloss, and Pass B provides a polished translation that correctly identifies the scripture references (Luke 16:13 and Matthew 22:21) alluded to in the Latin. The translation of 'pellicis dolor' as 'pain of flaying' in Pass B is a valid interpretation of the Latin context regarding skin/hide. The translation of 'cadaveribus' as 'corpses' in Pass B is correct.
